# Acceptance rules (addendum)

## Files and paths
Four output files are required, each read at its declared path relative to the supplied output root (no extra directory layer, no fallback search):

- `hrv_time.csv` — time-domain indices
- `hrv_freq.csv` — frequency-domain indices (PSD normalized by maximum)
- `hrv_nonlinear.csv` — non-linear indices
- `hrv_indices.csv` — combined all-domain table

Any missing file, unreadable file, or file placed at any other path (including under an extra `outputs/` subdirectory) fails the corresponding checks.

## File format
Each file is a comma-separated UTF-8 text file: one header row of `HRV_` index names followed by exactly one data row, with no index column. Any other shape (no data row, more than one data row, ragged row, extra blank line after the single record ends, duplicated or empty header names) fails the structural check. Quoted fields are decoded with standard CSV rules. Every data field must be either an empty field or a decimal numeric literal that parses to a finite value; `NaN`, `inf`, nonfinite tokens, and any non-numeric content fail. Column order within the header is not graded; column identity is by exact case-sensitive `HRV_` index name.

## Column sets
For each file, the set of column names must equal the reference set for that file exactly: every reference index present (no missing values masked by omission), no extra columns, and no renamed indices. The reference sets are the NeuroKit2-0.2.13 default index sets for this input: 25 columns in `hrv_time.csv` (`HRV_MeanNN` through `HRV_TINN`), 10 in `hrv_freq.csv` (`HRV_ULF` through `HRV_LnHF`), 60 in `hrv_nonlinear.csv`, and 95 in `hrv_indices.csv` (the column union of the three domain files; no respiration-derived indices).

## Undefined indices (empty fields)
Indices that the reference computation returns as undefined for a 5-minute recording — `HRV_ULF`, `HRV_SDANN2`, `HRV_SDNNI2`, `HRV_SDANN5`, `HRV_SDNNI5` — must be written as empty fields. Zero, `NaN`, or any numeric substitute in place of an undefined index fails, as does reporting a value in the reference-position empty field. Conversely, every index with a reference value must carry a numeric field; an empty field there fails.

## Numeric comparison
Values are compared after parsing, on the decoded scientific value, per column matched by index name.

A submission value `s` matches the reference value `r` when

  |s − r| ≤ 1e-9 + 1e-9 · |r|   (reference value as denominator; both sides in the same reported units)

This bound is a limit on observable output differences. It accepts small serialization/hand-off round-off of the written decimal representation (an ordinary CSV write/read round trip of the reported values must not change grading), but any deviation beyond it — including one milli in a millisecond-unit index, a percent-level change produced by different preprocessing settings (e.g. artifact-corrected or substituted R peaks, unnormalized PSD, different entropy tolerance or DFA window settings), or values from a different beat population — fails. The comparison is symmetric in absolute terms but anchored to the reference magnitude; scientific quantities are compared in the units stated for each index (milliseconds for NN-based time-domain indices, dimensionless normalized powers/ratios for frequency and non-linear domains).

Empty-field positions must match exactly; a submission with a value where the reference is undefined, or an empty field where the reference has a value, fails regardless of the numeric comparison.

## Cross-file consistency
`hrv_indices.csv` is graded against the submission's own three domain files: its column set must equal the union of the submission's `hrv_time.csv`, `hrv_freq.csv` and `hrv_nonlinear.csv` column sets, and each shared index must carry the same value, under the same numeric rule, as in the corresponding domain file (empty-field status included). The three domain files must also be mutually consistent on any index name they share. A correct-looking combined table cannot compensate for value errors in the domain files; each file is graded separately, and every check must pass.

## Verdict
All checks (structure, the four per-file value checks, and cross-file consistency) must pass. The grader reports pass/fail per check and always exits 0 after writing its report; a crash or malformed submission is a failed check, not a successful run.
candidate.rationale:
## What is compared
The four declared single-row CSVs are graded on parsed scientific content: exact per-file column-name sets matched by case-sensitive HRV_ index name, empty-field positions for the undefined 5-minute indices (HRV_ULF, HRV_SDANN2/SDNNI2/SDANN5/SDNNI5), and per-index numeric values, plus a cross-file consistency check tying hrv_indices.csv to the union of the submission's three domain files. Reference values are read dynamically from the reference directory; no answers, column lists, or hashes are embedded (the counts quoted in the addendum come from the reference observations and are stated for transparency, not enforced as literals).

## Numerical rule and its justification
Tolerance |s-r| <= 1e-9 + 1e-9*|r| with the reference value as denominator (relative anchor). Justification: the reference is the NeuroKit2-0.2.13 default pipeline on a pinned stack, and every executed control reproduces the four files byte-identically (reference, oracle recomputation, independent solution, two repeatability replays, all sha256-identical), so no recomputation noise needs to be absorbed by the comparison. The bound still covers ordinary serialization round-off at the CSV hand-off boundary: a control run in this session confirmed that a pandas read→write round trip (the file's own short-repr decimals, i.e. a shortest round-trip representation) passes, and a file with a 1e-13 absolute perturbation passes while a 1e-3 perturbation fails. The bound tolerance exercised textually is far below any meaningful scientific difference in the reported units (ms indices, normalized powers, entropies), so different preprocessing settings (artifact-corrected or substituted peaks, unnormalized PSD, different entropy tolerance/DFA windows) or a different beat population fail. Cross-version portability (different numpy/scipy/pandas stacks) was NOT tested: the sandbox could not install another stack (no pip, offline; the only available environment is the pinned one), so independent evidence for a wider tolerance is absent; the boundary was exercised with synthetic controls, which is representation-only evidence, not recomputation evidence, and the addendum states the tolerance as an observable-difference limit, not a method-detection guarantee.

## Encoding facts (observed)
- Files are comma-separated with a header row, one data row, no index column, trailing newline, pandas-default float formatting; empty fields (e.g. ",,," for the undefined indices) verified by direct inspection of the reference CSVs.
- Undefined semantics: NeuroKit2 leaves NaN for indices requiring longer recordings and 5-minute ULF, exported as empty fields; the grader requires empty fields exactly at those positions and rejects zero/NaN substitutes (control: zeros-filled submission fails).
- 1 data row per file; extra data rows, ragged rows, duplicate headers all fail the structural check (control: empty submission fails all checks with a valid report and exit 0).

## Check structure
Six checks: one structural (CSV shape, finiteness, format), four scientific per-file value checks (time, frequency, non-linear, combined) and one scientific cross-file consistency check (combined table = column union of the submission's domain files with matching values). This covers every required endpoint scientifically; no branch is hidden behind a schema check. Column order is not graded (name-keyed), since the notebook's export order is an arbitrary implementation detail, but column identity (exact names) is graded, so renaming cannot pass.

## Executed validation summary (this session)
Reference: passes all six. Empty submission: fails all six. Pandas round-trip: passes. Zeros for undefined: fails. 5% perturbation of HRV_RMSSD: fails the file check and cross-file consistency. Renamed column: fails. 1e-13 perturbation: passes; 1e-3 perturbation: fails. Report schema verified to contain exactly {"passed", "checks"} with check objects {"id", "passed", "message"}.

## Limitations
- No cross-version numerical drift measurement was possible (only the pinned stack is installable here); the tolerance rests on serialization arguments and the executed round-trip controls, not on multi-stack recomputation.
- The trusted input (BIOTASKS_TRUSTED_INPUT_DIR) is not needed by the comparator because every acceptance-affecting relation is determined by the reference tables themselves (column identities, empty positions, values); the input is implicitly exercised through the reference outputs and the value checks.
- Independent mutation-suite coverage (e.g. sampling-rate shifts, cleaned-peak variants) is owned by the separate worker; local controls here are consistent with rejecting those classes via the identity/value checks described above.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""HRV indices for a 5-minute resting ECG recording.

Pipeline (NeuroKit2 0.2.13 defaults):
  1. R-peak detection on the raw ECG column with the default "neurokit"
     finder at sampling_rate=100, correct_artifacts=False (no artifact
     correction, no pre-cleaning, no substituted detector).
  2. NN interval series (ms) from the detected peak indices at 100 Hz.
  3. nk.hrv_time, nk.hrv_frequency (normalize=True, Welch interpolation
     onto a 100 Hz grid), nk.hrv_nonlinear at default settings, and the
     combined nk.hrv table (column-wise concatenation of the three
     domains; no RSP-derived indices).

Undefined indices (e.g. HRV_ULF, SDANN2/SDNNI2/SDANN5/SDNNI5 for a
5-minute recording) are written as empty CSV fields via na_rep="".
"""
import argparse
import os

import pandas as pd
import neurokit2 as nk


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--input-dir", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--output-dir", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    data = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(args.input_dir, "bio_resting_5min_100hz.csv"))
    ecg = data["ECG"]
    sampling_rate = 100

    # Step 1: R-peak detection, default "neurokit" finder, raw ECG,
    # no artifact correction.
    _, info = nk.ecg_peaks(
        ecg,
        sampling_rate=sampling_rate,
        method="neurokit",
        correct_artifacts=False,
    )
    peaks = info["ECG_R_Peaks"]

    os.makedirs(args.output_dir, exist_ok=True)

    # Steps 2-6: domain computations at the reference preset defaults.
    hrv_t = nk.hrv_time(peaks, sampling_rate=sampling_rate)
    hrv_f = nk.hrv_frequency(peaks, sampling_rate=sampling_rate, normalize=True)
    hrv_n = nk.hrv_nonlinear(peaks, sampling_rate=sampling_rate)
    # Combined table: domain functions at default settings (PSD
    # normalization on), concatenated column-wise; no RSP columns passed.
    hrv_all = nk.hrv(peaks, sampling_rate=sampling_rate)

    for frame, filename in (
        (hrv_t, "hrv_time.csv"),
        (hrv_f, "hrv_freq.csv"),
        (hrv_n, "hrv_nonlinear.csv"),
        (hrv_all, "hrv_indices.csv"),
    ):
        frame.to_csv(
            os.path.join(args.output_dir, filename),
            index=False,
            na_rep="",  # undefined indices -> empty fields
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Materialize supplied inputs and reference projections for the HRV task.

Reads the manifest of original absolute input paths, copies the original
recording byte-for-byte into destination/inputs/, and copies the original
terminal reference artifacts (the four HRV CSVs produced by the recorded
source execution) unchanged into destination/reference/.
"""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import os
import shutil

INPUT_BASENAME = "bio_resting_5min_100hz.csv"
REFERENCE_OUTPUTS = ["hrv_time.csv", "hrv_freq.csv", "hrv_nonlinear.csv", "hrv_indices.csv"]


def sha256(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: fh.read(1 << 20), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()


def find_original_input(manifest):
    """Locate the absolute local path of the original recording in the manifest.

    The manifest references original absolute input paths anywhere in its JSON
    structure. Collect candidate existing files whose basename matches the
    known input filename; prefer the staging location under /inputs/.
    """
    found = []

    def walk(node):
        if isinstance(node, str):
            if os.path.basename(node) == INPUT_BASENAME and os.path.isfile(node):
                found.append(node)
        elif isinstance(node, dict):
            for v in node.values():
                walk(v)
        elif isinstance(node, list):
            for v in node:
                walk(v)

    walk(manifest)
    if not found:
        raise SystemExit("Could not locate %s in manifest" % INPUT_BASENAME)
    unique = sorted(set(found))
    preferred = [p for p in unique if os.sep + "inputs" + os.sep in p]
    selected = preferred[0] if len(preferred) == 1 else (unique[0] if len(unique) == 1 else None)
    if selected is None:
        raise SystemExit("Ambiguous matches for %s: %s" % (INPUT_BASENAME, unique))
    return selected


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--source-inputs", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--reference-dir", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--destination", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    with open(args.source_inputs, "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        manifest = json.load(fh)

    inputs_dir = os.path.join(args.destination, "inputs")
    reference_dir = os.path.join(args.destination, "reference")
    os.makedirs(inputs_dir, exist_ok=True)
    os.makedirs(reference_dir, exist_ok=True)

    # Copy original task data byte-for-byte.
    src = find_original_input(manifest)
    dst = os.path.join(inputs_dir, INPUT_BASENAME)
    shutil.copyfile(src, dst)
    if sha256(src) != sha256(dst):
        raise SystemExit("Byte-identity check failed for staged input")

    # Project the recorded reference answer artifacts unchanged (no recovery
    # needed: all four endpoints were exported by the original execution).
    for name in REFERENCE_OUTPUTS:
        rsrc = os.path.join(args.reference_dir, name)
        if not os.path.isfile(rsrc):
            raise SystemExit("Missing reference artifact: %s" % rsrc)
        rdst = os.path.join(reference_dir, name)
        shutil.copyfile(rsrc, rdst)
        if sha256(rsrc) != sha256(rdst):
            raise SystemExit("Byte-identity check failed for %s" % name)

    print(json.dumps({
        "staged_input": INPUT_BASENAME,
        "input_sha256": sha256(dst),
        "reference_artifacts": REFERENCE_OUTPUTS,
        "reference_sha256": {n: sha256(os.path.join(reference_dir, n)) for n in REFERENCE_OUTPUTS},
    }, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Heart rate variability (HRV) indices for a 5-minute resting ECG recording

## Objective

You are given a 5-minute multi-channel physiological recording of a participant at rest (ECG, PPG, RSP), sampled at 100 Hz. Using the **ECG channel**, determine R-peak occurrences, derive the R–R (NN) interval series, and compute the participant's heart-rate-variability indices in the time domain, the frequency domain, the non-linear domain, and as a combined all-domain summary.

The reference pipeline is the standard, default HRV computation of **NeuroKit2 version 0.2.13** (`nk.hrv_time`, `nk.hrv_frequency` with `normalize=True`, `nk.hrv_nonlinear`, `nk.hrv` with `sampling_rate=100`). A reference execution environment (Python 3.13 with `neurokit2==0.2.13`, `numpy==2.5.4`, `scipy==1.18.1`, `pandas==2.3.3`) is available in the sandbox for convenience, but you may use any implementation that produces the requested quantities. Output values must be reported for the same indices, with the same definitions, as this preset.

## Input

`inputs/bio_resting_5min_100hz.csv` — a comma-separated file with a header row and three numeric columns `ECG`, `PPG`, `RSP`, giving samples of a resting recording at **100 Hz** (consecutive rows are consecutive samples, 10 ms apart; 30,000 rows). Use the `ECG` column only.

## Method

1. **R-peak detection.** Detect R-peak sample indices in the raw ECG column with the default NeuroKit2 R-peak finder (`method="neurokit"`), at `sampling_rate=100`. Do **not** apply artifact correction to the detected peaks (`correct_artifacts=False`) and do not substitute a different detector or a pre-cleaned series; the detected peak set defines the beat population for all subsequent indices.
2. **R–R intervals.** From the detected peak indices, form the successive-difference NN interval series in **milliseconds**, based on the 100 Hz sampling.
3. **Time-domain indices.** Compute the standard time-domain HRV statistics of the NN series (ms units): mean (MeanNN), standard deviation (SDNN), RMSSD/SDSD, coefficient-of-variation indices, median/MAD/IQR, 20th/80th percentiles, pNN50/pNN20 (percent of successive differences exceeding 50 ms / 20 ms), minimum/maximum NN, Henrich triangle index and TINN, and the SDANN/SDNNI statistics over **1-minute** windows. Indices that require longer recordings than 5 minutes (SDANN2, SDNNI2, SDANN5, SDNNI5) are undefined for this input and must be reported as empty.
4. **Frequency-domain indices.** Interpolate the NN series onto a uniform 100 Hz grid, estimate the power spectral density with **Welch's method** (Hann window, mean averaging, spectral density scaling, no per-segment detrending), **normalize the PSD by its maximum value**, and integrate band power over: ULF 0–0.0033 Hz (undefined for a 5-minute recording → empty), VLF 0.0033–0.04 Hz, LF 0.04–0.15 Hz, HF 0.15–0.4 Hz, VHF 0.4–0.5 Hz. # # Heart Rate Variability (HRV)

# NeuroKit2 is the most comprehensive package when it comes to HRV indices, and this example shows how to use NeuroKit2 to compute heart rate variability (HRV) indices in the time-, frequency-, and non-linear domain.
#
# For a comprehensive review of the most up-to-date HRV indices, a discussion of their significance in psychology, and a step-by-step guide for HRV analysis using **NeuroKit2**, the [Heart Rate Variability in Psychology: A Review of HRV Indices and an Analysis Tutorial](https://doi.org/10.3390/s21123998) paper is a good place to start. 

# ## Compute HRV features

# Load the NeuroKit package
import neurokit2 as nk

# Note: this cell is hidden using the "remove-input" tag
# Make bigger images
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = [15, 5]
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 14

# ## Download Dataset

# First, let's download the resting rate data (sampled at 100Hz) using `nk.data()`.

data = nk.data("bio_resting_5min_100hz")
data.head()  # Print first 5 rows

# You can see that it consists of three different signals, pertaining to ECG, PPG (an alternative determinant of heart rate as compared to ECG), and RSP (respiration). Now, let's extract the ECG signal in the shape of a vector (i.e., a one-dimensional array), and find the peaks using [ecg_peaks()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/ecg.html#ecg-peaks).

# Find peaks
peaks, info = nk.ecg_peaks(data["ECG"], sampling_rate=100)

# *Note: It is critical that you specify the correct sampling rate of your signal throughout many processing functions, as this allows NeuroKit to have a time reference.*

# This produces two elements, `peaks` which is a DataFrame of same length as the input signal in which occurences of R-peaks are marked with 1 in a list of zeros. `info` is a dictionary of the sample points at which these R-peaks occur. 
#
# HRV is the temporal variation between consecutive heartbeats (**RR intervals**). Here, we will use `peaks` i.e. occurrences of the heartbeat peaks, as the input argument in the following HRV functions to extract the indices. 

# ## Time-Domain Analysis

# First, let's extract the time-domain indices.

# Extract clean EDA and SCR features
hrv_time = nk.hrv_time(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_time

# These features include the RMSSD (square root of the mean of the sum of successive differences between adjacent RR intervals), MeanNN (mean of RR intervals) so on and so forth. You can also visualize the distribution of R-R intervals by specifying `show=True` in [hrv_time()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-time).

# ## Frequency-Domain Analysis

# Now, let's extract the frequency domain features, which involve extracting for example the spectral power density pertaining to different frequency bands. Again, you can visualize the power across frequency bands by specifying `show=True` in [hrv_frequency()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-frequency).

hrv_freq = nk.hrv_frequency(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True, normalize=True)
hrv_freq

# ## Non-Linear Domain Analysis

# Now, let's compute the non-linear indices with [hrv_nonlinear()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-nonlinear).

hrv_nonlinear = nk.hrv_nonlinear(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_nonlinear

# This will produce a Poincaré plot which plots each RR interval against the next successive one.
#
# Note that there exist many more [**complexity indices**](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/complexity.html), that are available in NeuroKit2, and that could be applied to HRV. The ``hrv_nonlinear()`` function only includes the most commonly used indices.

# ## All Domains

# Finally, if you'd like to extract HRV indices from all three domains, you can simply input `peaks` into [hrv()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html), where you can specify `show=True` to visualize the combination of plots depicting the RR intervals distribution, power spectral density for frequency domains, and the poincare scattergram.

hrv_indices = nk.hrv(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_indices

specification.task_brief:
# Heart rate variability (HRV) indices for a 5-minute resting ECG recording

## Objective

You are given a 5-minute multi-channel physiological recording of a participant at rest (ECG, PPG, RSP), sampled at 100 Hz. Using the **ECG channel**, determine R-peak occurrences, derive the R–R (NN) interval series, and compute the participant's heart-rate-variability indices in the time domain, the frequency domain, the non-linear domain, and as a combined all-domain summary.

The reference pipeline is the standard, default HRV computation of **NeuroKit2 version 0.2.13** (`nk.hrv_time`, `nk.hrv_frequency` with `normalize=True`, `nk.hrv_nonlinear`, `nk.hrv` with `sampling_rate=100`). A reference execution environment (Python 3.13 with `neurokit2==0.2.13`, `numpy==2.5.4`, `scipy==1.18.1`, `pandas==2.3.3`) is available in the sandbox for convenience, but you may use any implementation that produces the requested quantities. Output values must be reported for the same indices, with the same definitions, as this preset.

## Input

`inputs/bio_resting_5min_100hz.csv` — a comma-separated file with a header row and three numeric columns `ECG`, `PPG`, `RSP`, giving samples of a resting recording at **100 Hz** (consecutive rows are consecutive samples, 10 ms apart; 30,000 rows). Use the `ECG` column only.

## Method

1. **R-peak detection.** Detect R-peak sample indices in the raw ECG column with the default NeuroKit2 R-peak finder (`method="neurokit"`), at `sampling_rate=100`. Do **not** apply artifact correction to the detected peaks (`correct_artifacts=False`) and do not substitute a different detector or a pre-cleaned series; the detected peak set defines the beat population for all subsequent indices.
2. **R–R intervals.** From the detected peak indices, form the successive-difference NN interval series in **milliseconds**, based on the 100 Hz sampling.
3. **Time-domain indices.** Compute the standard time-domain HRV statistics of the NN series (ms units): mean (MeanNN), standard deviation (SDNN), RMSSD/SDSD, coefficient-of-variation indices, median/MAD/IQR, 20th/80th percentiles, pNN50/pNN20 (percent of successive differences exceeding 50 ms / 20 ms), minimum/maximum NN, Henrich triangle index and TINN, and the SDANN/SDNNI statistics over **1-minute** windows. Indices that require longer recordings than 5 minutes (SDANN2, SDNNI2, SDANN5, SDNNI5) are undefined for this input and must be reported as empty.
4. **Frequency-domain indices.** Interpolate the NN series onto a uniform 100 Hz grid, estimate the power spectral density with **Welch's method** (Hann window, mean averaging, spectral density scaling, no per-segment detrending), **normalize the PSD by its maximum value**, and integrate band power over: ULF 0–0.0033 Hz (undefined for a 5-minute recording → empty), VLF 0.0033–0.04 Hz, LF 0.04–0.15 Hz, HF 0.15–0.4 Hz, VHF 0.4–0.5 Hz. Report the band powers, the total power (sum over the bands), the LF/HF ratio, the LF and HF fractions of total power (`LFn`, `HFn`), and the natural logarithm of HF power (`LnHF`).
5. **Non-linear indices.** Compute the standard default non-linear indices of the NN series: Poincaré SD1, SD2, their ratio and ellipse area; CSI, CVI and modified CSI; PIP, IALS, PSS, PAS; Guzik and Porta indices (GI, SI, AI, PI); asymmetric Poincaré decomposition (C1d/C1a, SD1d/SD1a, C2d/C2a, SD2d/SD2a, Cd/Ca, SDNNd/SDNNa); DFA short- and long-term scaling exponents (alpha1, alpha2) and the multifractal-DFA alpha1/alpha2 summary statistics (Width, Peak, Mean, Max, Delta, Asymmetry, Fluctuation, Increment); approximate, sample, Shannon, fuzzy and multiscale entropies (ApEn, SampEn, ShanEn, FuzzyEn, MSEn, CMSEn, RCMSEn); correlation dimension (CD), Higuchi and Katz fractal dimensions (HFD, KFD), Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZC), and the equal-probability 4-symbol symbolic-dynamics proportions (0V, 1V, 2LV, 2UV patterns).
6. **Combined table.** Produce the same three domain outputs obtained from the domain functions used at their **default settings** (including PSD normalization at the default) and concatenate them column-wise into one table. No respiration-derived indices are included (no RSP columns are passed).

For any index whose NeuroKit2-0.2.13 default settings matter (entropy tolerance `r`, DFA window ranges, MST/max-scale for multiscale entropy, symbolic pattern length), the reference preset's defaults — not the original literature conventions — define the requested quantity.

## Outputs

Write four comma-separated files (header row of index names, one value row, no index column), with empty fields for undefined indices:

- `outputs/hrv_time.csv` — the time-domain indices.
- `outputs/hrv_freq.csv` — the frequency-domain indices (with PSD normalized by maximum, as above).
- `outputs/hrv_nonlinear.csv` — the non-linear indices.
- `outputs/hrv_indices.csv` — the combined table of the three domains at default settings.

Index names follow the `HRV_` prefix convention of the reference preset (e.g., `HRV_MeanNN`, `HRV_RMSSD`, `HRV_LF`, `HRV_SD1`, `HRV_SampEn`). Each output must report a value (or an empty field, where undefined) for every index that the reference preset's default computation returns for this input.

## Resources

Offline execution, 4 CPUs, 8 GiB RAM, ≤ 10 GiB disk; your program must finish within 600 seconds. Reference execution of this analysis completes in well under one minute on the provided environment.
